name: Garlic / ginseng / aloe scalp remedies

card.summary: Folk plant remedies for the scalp, with no hair-growth trials found and documented burn reports for raw garlic.
card.note: Raw garlic on skin has been linked to burns.

quick.overview:
Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are among the plant ingredients people apply to the scalp as home remedies for hair loss.
No hair-growth studies of them exist.
quick.mechanism: Users apply juices, gels or extracts to the scalp, usually describing a stimulating or soothing effect. No mechanism for hair growth has been established.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports burns from topical garlic and possible rash or allergy from aloe gel. Ginseng has listed side effects when taken orally.

lead: Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are among the best-known plant ingredients people use on or for the scalp in pursuit of thicker, healthier-looking hair. Garlic is rubbed on or blended into oils and gels, ginseng appears in hair-care products and as an oral extract, and aloe gel is used as a soothing, conditioning scalp treatment and is a common shampoo ingredient [1][2][3].

All three have long histories in traditional medicine: garlic across Korea, Egypt, Japan, China, Rome and Greece, ginseng in East Asian folk medicine, and aloe as a skin remedy in records going back to the fourth millennium BCE [1][2][3]. In hair-loss discussion they sit in the broader group of natural remedies, alongside the medical options of minoxidil and finasteride [13].

Hair-specific research is small. A 2007 double-blind trial of 40 people with localised alopecia areata tested garlic gel added to a steroid cream, and a 2009 Korean trial of oral Korean red ginseng in androgenic alopecia reported increases in hair density and thickness [4][5]. Wikipedia's hair-loss article states that evidence for aloe vera and ginseng was insufficient as of 2011 [13].

chain: Plant juice, gel or extract applied to the scalp or taken by mouth
Soothes or stimulates the scalp; some extracts studied for hair density
angle.text: Users apply garlic, aloe gel or ginseng products to the scalp, or take ginseng orally, hoping for denser, healthier-looking hair. Small trials have examined garlic gel in alopecia areata and red ginseng in pattern hair loss.

infobox: Garlic (Allium sativum), ginseng (Panax ginseng), aloe vera
Garlic gel in alopecia areata (2007); Korean red ginseng in androgenic alopecia (2009) [4][5]
Pattern hair loss, patchy hair loss, dry or irritated scalp

sections.h: How people use them for hair
paras: Home preparations include crushed garlic or garlic-infused oil massaged into the scalp, aloe gel scooped from the leaf and used as a scalp mask or leave-in conditioner, and ginseng extracts in tonics, shampoos and capsules. Proponents describe the aim as stimulating the scalp, calming irritation and giving hair a thicker, shinier appearance. These are common in natural-hair and traditional-medicine circles; looksmaxxing forums discuss them far less than minoxidil or finasteride, which are the standard options for pattern hair loss [13].

Pattern hair loss affects about half of men and a quarter of women by age 50, and alopecia areata, an autoimmune patchy loss, affects about 2 percent of people at some point, which is part of why people look for gentler or kitchen-cupboard options [13][14].

Crushing garlic releases enzymes that form allicin and other sulfur compounds, responsible for its sharp taste and odour [1]. Garlic has a long record in traditional medicine; Pliny the Elder listed conditions it was thought to help and Galen called it a cure-all [1].

Garlic has been applied to skin in naturopathic practice and for acne. Wikipedia reports serious burns from raw garlic on skin, including in children, and advises testing a small area at low concentration, discouraging topical use of raw garlic [1].
For hair, the best-known study tested garlic gel together with betamethasone valerate cream in alopecia areata over three months [4].

Panax ginseng is a perennial native to the Russian Far East, Northeast China and the Korean Peninsula, with roots harvested at about five or six years; Pierre Jartoux described the name 'gin-seng' in 1711 [2]. Wikipedia says ginsenosides are under preliminary research and that evidence of health effects is limited; its listed side effects include headache, raised blood pressure, insomnia and rash, and it can interact with warfarin [2].

Korean red ginseng is steamed ginseng root. The 2009 trial authors noted that red ginseng has been reported to stimulate hair follicles and is already used in hair products [5]. Reviews describe ginseng among plant adaptogens, extracts historically used to raise stability against physical loads [6].

Aloe leaves contain the polysaccharide gel acemannan along with lignans, sterols and polyphenols, and the gel is mildly acidic [3]. Cosmetic makers add aloe to shampoos, moisturisers and shaving cream, which a literature review attributes to a moisturising, emollient effect [3].

Wikipedia describes the evidence for aloe on wounds and burns as conflicting, notes topical use is generally not associated with significant side effects, and lists contact dermatitis among possible allergic reactions [3]. The article does not discuss specific hair benefits [3].

Two small randomised trials have looked at hair outcomes. In a double-blind study by Hajheydari and colleagues, 40 people with localised alopecia areata applied garlic gel or placebo gel twice daily alongside betamethasone valerate cream for three months. Nineteen of 20 in the garlic group had a good response versus a significantly lower rate in the control group, with no complications observed; the authors suggested garlic gel may be a useful adjunct [4].

In a trial by Kim and colleagues in the Journal of Ginseng Research (2009), Korean red ginseng extract or placebo was taken by mouth for 24 weeks by people with androgenic alopecia. Hair count, thickness and density were measured with a Folliscope; the authors reported increased density and thickness, higher patient satisfaction and supportive dermatologist photo ratings [5]. Different abstracts of the paper give 40 or 32 participants.
No trial of aloe vera for hair growth was found. Other research on these plants covers other outcomes, such as garlic and blood pressure and ginseng and cognition [11][12].

Topical raw garlic has been linked to burns, and garlic supplements may add to bleeding risk with anticoagulants [1][7][8]. Aloe gel can cause rash or allergic reaction, oral whole-leaf aloe extract has been classified by the IARC as a possible carcinogen, and aloe should not be used in pregnancy [3]. Oral ginseng has listed side effects and drug interactions [2]. Patients with autoimmune hair loss are commonly managed with steroids, minoxidil or newer JAK inhibitors under medical care [14].

On looksmax.org, garlic appears mainly as a food thought to raise testosterone; one poster ate raw cloves for that reason and described nausea and a burning mouth, and a reply called it a meme [9][10]. Scalp use of these plants is a minor theme compared with discussion of prescription hair-loss treatments [13].

timeline.event: Earliest records of aloe as a skin treatment [3].
Pierre Jartoux describes ginseng's Chinese name 'gin-seng' for European readers [2].
Double-blind trial reports topical garlic gel added to betamethasone in alopecia areata [4].
Korean trial of oral Korean red ginseng in androgenic alopecia published in the Journal of Ginseng Research [5].
IARC classifies aloe vera whole-leaf extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans [3].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, garlic is discussed mostly as a food said to raise testosterone; plant remedies for scalp hair appear less often [9][10].

claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster ate raw cloves because they had read they increase testosterone, and a satirical reply called garlic the ultimate T-boosting food [10].
claims.experts: Another poster replied that it is a meme [9]. No testosterone trials have been published.

claims.claim: Garlic applied to the scalp helps hair regrow
claims.believers: Proponents of natural remedies apply garlic preparations hoping for regrowth.
claims.experts: One double-blind trial found garlic gel plus betamethasone improved alopecia areata more than placebo plus betamethasone [4]; Wikipedia warns of burns from raw garlic on skin [1].

claims.believers: Users take ginseng as a supplement for hair density, citing its folk reputation for stimulating follicles [5].
claims.experts: A 2009 trial reported increased density and thickness over 24 weeks [5]; Wikipedia's hair-loss article considers ginseng evidence insufficient [13].

claims.claim: Aloe gel nourishes and conditions the scalp
claims.believers: Users apply aloe as a soothing scalp mask and conditioner.
claims.experts: Aloe is added to shampoos for a moisturising effect [3]; no hair-growth trial was found.

claims.claim: Plant remedies are a gentler alternative to finasteride and minoxidil
claims.believers: Natural-remedy advocates prefer plant products to drugs with side effects.
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists minoxidil and finasteride as the evidence-based treatments for pattern loss and describes herbal options as insufficiently evidenced [13].
